bibliographic.title: Deep soccer analytics: learning an action-value function for evaluating soccer players

scope.rationale: Paper develops a Deep Reinforcement Learning model to learn an action-value Q-function for evaluating all types of on-the-ball soccer actions from event data, and derives the Goal Impact Metric (GIM) player ranking. Directly within SAVANT's action-valuation scope.

model.name: Two-Tower Dynamic Play LSTM (TTDP-LSTM) with Goal Impact Metric (GIM)
inputs: play history sequence (s_t, a_{t-1}, x_{t-1}, ..., x_0)
model.target: Q_team(s,a) = P(goal_team = 1 | s_t = s, a_t = a): probability that team (Home/Away/Neither) scores the next goal given current state and action
model.architecture: Two-tower stacked LSTM (one tower per home/away team); each tower is a two-layer LSTM with 256 hidden nodes plus an embedding layer and two hidden layers with 256 nodes; outputs normalized via softmax to produce Q_Home, Q_Away, Q_Neither; trained with on-policy Temporal Difference (Sarsa) and a dynamic-possession LSTM trace length (max 10 steps); Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 10E-04 (general) and 10E-05 (fine-tuning). Interpretability via CART mimic regression tree.
model.temporal_horizon: until end of current goal-scoring episode (next goal or end of game)

metrics: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between estimated and empirical scoring probabilities
Correlation with standard success measures (Goals, Assists, Shots per Game, Pass Success percentage, Key Passes per game, Yellow cards, Red cards)
Round-by-round correlation with season totals (assists, goals)
Paired t-test (significance test between player evaluation metrics)
baselines: Scoring Impact (SI) (Schulte et al. 2017a Markov model)
evaluation.splits: Not explicitly described as train/val/test splits; model is fit on the full 2017-2018 multi-league dataset (over 4.5M events) with fine-tuning on EFL Championship league-specific data. No explicit match-level holdout described.

claims.statement: The trained TTDP-LSTM achieves average MAE below 0.1 for all bins of context features (Manpower, Goal Differential, Period), significantly outperforming the discrete-state Markov Model baseline.

GIM achieves the highest correlation with 4 out of 5 positive success measures (Goals 0.844, Assists 0.498, SpG 0.596, KeyP 0.562) over players in all 10 leagues; only GIM and M-GIM show negative correlations with yellow/red cards.

Fine-tuned FT-GIM achieves the highest correlations with Goals (0.736), Assists (0.585), SpG (0.569) and KeyP (0.592) for EFL Championship players, and the largest negative correlations with Yellow (-0.110) and Red (-0.171) cards.

Significance test (paired t-tests) rejects the null that GIM equals other player evaluation metrics with p-values 9.33E-2, 5.27E-281, 8.03*E-218, 4.82E-14 and 1.02E-118 for PlusMinus, XG, SI, VAEP and M-GIM respectively.
Proposition 1: For each player i, his Q-value-above-replacement equals his goal impact metric (QAAR^i(D) = GIM^i(D)), unifying the two fundamental approaches to player evaluation in an RL framework.
The dataset contains 4,679,354 events, 5,510 players, 2,976 games, 164 teams across 10 European leagues in the 2017-18 season.
Top-ranked player by GIM over the EFL Championship 2017-2018 season is Matej Vydra (GIM=18.017, 21 goals, 4 assists), who won the 2017-18 Golden Boot and was signed by Burnley the next season.

Spatial Q-value generalization shows that shot, pass, and cross Q-values increase with proximity to the opponent's goal, while defensive tackling Q-value increases with proximity to the team's own goal.

TTDP-LSTM training uses Adam optimizer with initial general learning rate 10E-04 over 4.5M events (4,386,894 gradient steps) and fine-tuning learning rate 10E-05 on EFL Championship data (818,120 gradient steps).

limitations: Partial observability: the dataset records only positions and actions of the on-the-ball player; positions of off-ball players are unknown. The recurrent model partially compensates by inferring missing information from history, but performance is still limited by partial observability.

Big input data problem: the dataset has over 4M events including spatial/temporal features, making it difficult to use standard machine learning packages that fit entire data in memory; future work will explore online learning methods.

Convergence of on-policy TD with non-linear (neural) function approximators is not theoretically guaranteed; the authors mitigate by constraining look-ahead to the next goal and removing the discount factor.
Sparsity of goals in soccer makes reinforcement-learning style training challenging; the TD solution propagates scoring signals to previous events to address goal sparsity.
open_questions: Building a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that combines fully observable tracking data with event categories, possibly by combining the deep RL tracking model of Dick and Brefeld (2019) with this event-based deep RL model.
Exploring on-line learning methods to improve scalability on large sports datasets and to update player assessments after every round.
Incorporating tracking data into the framework.
